machine.name: Apple M5 Pro
machine.reference: official BLAKE3 1.8.7: b3sum and the blake3 crate with NEON + rayon

status_note: Numbers from 2026-10-26. NVIDIA: Bend's CUDA runtime on Modal's B200 and L4, with its heap in 1 GiB pieces (Modal's sandbox grants no bigger managed allocation).

in_memory.note: Warm, data already in memory, same bytes and same digest. Rust = blake3 crate (NEON + rayon).

gpu_reference.note: Bend's GPU path (hash1!) against hand-written Metal (bend/ref), warm, in memory, same digest; medians of 6 interleaved rounds on a loaded machine (+-10%); the 1 GiB row is from after Bend's lanes began reading interleaved groups. metal_bend_leaves runs the native kernel in hash1!'s shape: one thread per leaf, ~16,384 leaves.

cli.note: One-shot `b3sum FILE...` (process start included), medians of 15 interleaved rounds; output byte-identical to the official b3sum.

daemon.note: A long-running process, start-up excluded: every round re-opens and re-reads the files and hashes them. Rust seq = one file at a time, as b3sum; Rust par = rayon across files (the strongest baseline). Bend GPU reads into reused blocks of a 4 GB Metal heap set up once, then hashes every file in one bang. Bend CPU loads in 8 parts and hashes each while the rest open. Medians of 21 rounds on a busy machine (load average ~18).

iroh.note: iroh-blobs 0.103 ingest (add_path: BLAKE3 + bao outboard, plus the store's own bookkeeping) into a fresh store, against Bend computing the same hash and the same outboard (byte-identical to bao-tree's) in a long-running process. Best of 5 rounds each.

floors: Page faults on a mapped file: ~15 ms per GiB, serialized in the kernel (shared by every tool).
All-core CPU ceiling near 38 GB/s for BLAKE3 on this chip (Rust and Bend both reach it).
macOS open(): ~48 ms per 10,000 files at best, however many threads (volume-wide serialization).
GPU start-up: the Metal heap costs ~50 ms per GiB to set up, so one-shot CLI runs stay on the CPU.

Uncached files: the SSD reads 10-14 GB/s with large parallel preads but 0.2-0.8 GB/s through page faults, so mapping a file that is not in the page cache throws most of the SSD away (Bend streams those).
NVIDIA GPUs: Bend 2.0.39's CUDA runtime hangs inside Modal's sandbox, even for the guide's pow2! example, while plain CUDA managed memory works there; NVIDIA numbers wait on that.
GPU reads: ~5.5-6.8 ms per GiB natively; BLAKE3's compressions fit under them, natively and in Bend, so the GPU hash is read-bound.

proofs.note: bend/prove.sh (bend PROOF.bend with a deep stack), one run on the M5 Pro at load 8-10: ALL PROOFS CHECK for 40 laws and 412 lemmas (ADR 0015). The known answers take most of it; the other laws check in about a minute. The 41st, span.nocarry (ADR 0014's follow-up), checks in under a second on its own.

techniques.title: BLAKE3 core in Bend2
techniques.summary: Unboxed U32 records compile to register code; Array<U32> is a packed buffer; Array.fork shares input down a parallel fork tree.
techniques.headline: BLAKE3, written in Bend2
techniques.dek: It starts here: a complete BLAKE3 in Bend2, a language that spreads tree-shaped work over every core. Its records compile to register code, so the compression function comes out like hand-written C.
points: Gives the official test vectors' answers
The baseline every later change is measured against

techniques.title: 8-lane compress8 + clang SLP
techniques.summary: Eight chunks per call, word-major lanes, one call site, SLP and inline flags: 2.95 GB/s per core vs NEON's 2.40.
techniques.headline: Eight blocks at a time, on every core
techniques.dek: Bend has no vector types, so its code is shaped until the C compiler packs eight BLAKE3 compressions into SIMD registers on its own. One core now outpaces the official crate's hand-written NEON.

techniques.title: b3sum I/O path
techniques.summary: Parallel one-pass loader, zero-copy read-only mmap, byte-balanced file tree, one write for all output.
techniques.headline: Thousands of files, hashed at once
techniques.dek: The command line opens, reads and hashes every file in parallel, maps big files instead of copying them, and writes all of its output in one go. The output is b3sum's, byte for byte.
points: Big files are read straight from the page cache, never copied
Work is balanced by bytes, so a few big files and many small ones share the cores evenly

techniques.title: Files past 4 GiB
techniques.summary: 1 GiB segments are complete BLAKE3 subtrees, hashed in parallel and merged as parents (past 4 TiB since the counter's high word landed).
techniques.headline: Movies and disk images welcome: files past 4 GiB
techniques.dek: Big files are hashed as 1 GiB pieces that fit BLAKE3's tree exactly, all in parallel, with the same fingerprint as the official tools. The command line stays on the CPU, where a one-shot run finishes first.
points: 13 files from 1 GiB to 8 GiB match the official b3sum
A 5 GiB file in 0.204 s, against b3sum's 0.219 s

techniques.title: Flat GPU leaves
techniques.summary: Fork-free 4/16/64-chunk leaves sized to the 16,384-lane cube: 93-110 GB/s on the GPU.
techniques.headline: The GPU hashes 1 GiB in 11.6 ms
techniques.dek: Each GPU thread now takes a whole run of chunks instead of one, sized so all 16,384 lanes stay busy. On an M5 Pro that is 2.4× the official crate on every CPU core.

stat.label: the official crate on every core, 1 GiB

techniques.title: Native GPU references
techniques.summary: Metal and CUDA BLAKE3 as yardsticks: native Metal hashes 1 GiB in ~6 ms. Bend's GPU path is read-bound: ~1.5x from its lane cube's memory locality, ~1.3x from its array reads.
techniques.headline: How fast can a GPU hash? A native yardstick
techniques.dek: Hand-written Metal and CUDA BLAKE3 kernels show what the hardware can do, and where Bend's GPU time goes: reading memory, not computing.

stat.label: native Metal on an M5 Pro, 1 GiB in 6.04 ms

techniques.title: Laws and proofs
techniques.summary: 20 laws the checker proves: official vectors computed by the checker, compress8 and par8 equal the scalar path lane by lane for every input, and BLAKE3's tree splits into 2^k segments and builds level by level, for any compression.
techniques.headline: Proven, not just tested
techniques.dek: BLAKE3 in Bend now ships with laws its compiler proves: the official answers, the eight-lane path equal to the plain one for every input, and the shape of the tree. If a proof breaks, the build says so.

techniques.title: Daemon race, map zone, iroh outboards
techniques.summary: Mapped files go into an address-space zone of their own (one munmap a round); the CPU tree also emits iroh-blobs' bao outboard, byte-identical to bao-tree.
techniques.headline: Built for services that hash all day
techniques.dek: Sync daemons and iroh nodes re-hash what they watch. A long-running turboblake keeps pace with the fastest parallel Rust we could write, and builds iroh's verified-streaming outboards on every core instead of one.

stat.label: iroh-blobs' own ingest of a 1 GiB file

techniques.title: Streaming and a GPU daemon
techniques.summary: Files not in the page cache stream in 1 GiB segments with 16 F_NOCACHE readers while Bend hashes (101.5 GB in ~7.6 s); a daemon refills reused GPU-heap blocks and hashes in one bang.
techniques.headline: A 101.5 GB model in about 8 seconds
techniques.dek: Model weights bigger than RAM used to crawl through page faults. Files that are not cached now stream straight off the SSD on 16 readers while every core hashes.

stat.label: a DeepSeek shard, official b3sum against turboblake

techniques.title: More laws: outboards, counts, streaming
techniques.summary: 28 laws now: the outboard tree gives the plain hash for every input, the tree over n chunks has n leaves and n - 1 parents, and the streaming merge stack builds BLAKE3's tree, every segment once and in order.
techniques.headline: Eight more laws, for the code that hashes big files
techniques.dek: The streaming and outboard paths behind the 101.5 GB result now carry proofs, not just tests: claims checked for every input, which no test suite can cover.

techniques.title: Strided GPU lanes; CPU + GPU on one input
techniques.summary: Past 512 MiB, lane l hashes 16-chunk groups l, l + S, l + 2S, l + 3S, so lanes running together read neighbouring memory: 1 GiB 13.2 -> 9.4 ms on the GPU. split.bend lets the CPU and the GPU hash one input at once by slices (13 of 16 on the GPU: 1 GiB in 8.0 ms, 1.06-1.12x the GPU alone).
techniques.headline: CPU and GPU, one file, at the same time
techniques.dek: Something the official Rust crate cannot do: the CPU cores and the GPU split one input and hash their parts together. GPU threads also read neighbouring memory now, which took 1 GiB from 13.2 to 9.4 ms.

stat.label: 1 GiB on an M5 Pro, CPU and GPU together

points: 6–12% faster than the GPU alone, measured on a busy machine

techniques.title: The engine as a library, every binding
techniques.summary: One hook in the official C and Rust (compress_subtree_to_parent_node) hands big subtrees to the Bend engine on its own thread; drop-ins for C, Rust, Python, Node, Bun, Deno, browsers and Go each run the tests of the package they replace.
techniques.headline: turboblake for Python, JavaScript, Go, C and Rust
techniques.dek: The engine is now a library, with a drop-in for the BLAKE3 package you already use: change the install line, keep your code. Each one passes the tests of the package it replaces.

stat.label: runtimes: C, Rust, Python, Node, Bun, Deno, browsers, Go

points: 1 GiB in about 40 ms from C, Python or Node: about 12× each one's default hash
Browsers get Bend's own JavaScript build

techniques.title: Native GPU kernels where they measure faster
techniques.summary: Hand-written CUDA and Metal run where they beat Bend's GPU path, beside the CPU + GPU split; Bend stays the CPU engine. SHA-256 measured on the same machines: 1 GiB in 574 ms, against 0.683 ms for native CUDA on a B200.
techniques.headline: Hand-written CUDA and Metal kernels join the engine
techniques.dek: turboblake no longer has to be Bend-only on the GPU: each machine runs whichever kernel measures faster. On an NVIDIA B200 the native kernel hashes 1 GiB in 0.683 ms.

stat.label: SHA-256 on the same B200 host, 1 GiB

points: Apple M5 Pro: native Metal hashes 1 GiB in 6.69 ms, 50× SHA-256
Bend stays the CPU engine, and the tree the proofs are about
The command line and the library run these kernels next

techniques.title: Files past 4 TiB
techniques.summary: Every span carries its chunk counter's high word, down to compress8, so files go past 2^32 chunks: a 4 TiB + 1 GiB file matches the official crate, at no measurable cost.
techniques.headline: No more “File too large”: files past 4 TiB
techniques.dek: Disk images, backups and dataset shards now pass 4 TiB. Where turboblake used to stop, it hashes on, with the same fingerprint as the official tools and no measurable cost.

stat.label: the new limit, about a million times higher

points: A 4.4 TB test file streamed in 241 s, identical to the official crate
The proofs cover both counter words, and the engine refuses any span that would need a carry

techniques.title: Proofs for every input
techniques.summary: The CPU, GPU and keyed trees are proven equal to the scalar tree for every array, span and both counter words, and that tree is BLAKE3's; the streaming loop as b3io runs it is BLAKE3's tree over a file's segments. 40 laws, 412 lemmas.
techniques.headline: Every hashing path, proven for every input
techniques.dek: The parts that turn your files into a hash were checked on 13 official test inputs. Now the CPU, GPU, keyed and streamed paths carry proofs that hold for every input and every file size, past 4 TiB included.
points: The CPU's and the GPU's trees are BLAKE3's tree, for every input
Keyed hashing and key derivation too
Streamed files: the loop that runs, for any size

techniques.title: Never slower than b3sum
techniques.summary: The hook takes only the subtrees the engine reads in place and wins; the engine's window covers the host's memory on macOS; stdin and --no-mmap read big blocks while the last one hashes; --check hashes a batch at a time. stdin 1 GiB 529 -> 57 ms, 2,000 x 64 KiB 10.9x, single files a tie.
techniques.headline: turboblake is never slower than b3sum
techniques.dek: We measured the command against the official b3sum case by case, found every place it lost, and fixed each one. Single files and every flag now tie; folders, pipes and --check got much faster.
points: 2,000 files of 64 KiB: 10.9× faster
--check: up to 2.9× faster
--keyed, --derive-key, --length, --seek: a tie

models.note: Real model weights from deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (MIT), one-shot b3sum FILE... on a 64 GB Mac, identical hashes. Files this size are mostly not in the page cache: the official b3sum reads them through page faults (16 KiB at a time); Bend checks residency and streams them in 1 GiB segments with large parallel preads while it hashes. The official b3sum took 526 s on its first run of the 101.5 GB shard.

On the Mac, CPU and GPU share one memory.
